source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module C unit 6 (courseware unit 18): deal structuring and financial strategies

facts.statement: Deal structuring and negotiation (courseware): a deal structure is the agreement between acquirer and target specifying their rights and obligations, reached through negotiation. Structuring decides how risk is shared and how many of the main objectives of both parties are achieved; the extent to which the acquirer takes on the target liabilities is one such point. The structure must also contain an acceptable amount of risk; containing risk in one place often moves it elsewhere (the courseware compares it to squeezing a water balloon). Main aspects: the acquisition vehicle and post-closing organisation, the form of acquisition, the form of payment and the legal form of the selling entity. Structure and financing are interwoven; tax issues, taxable and non-taxable structures, how the deal is financed and the role of private equity firms and hedge funds in financing leveraged deals all affect the agreement. The courseware describes the negotiating goal as a mutually beneficial (win-win) resolution.

Payment and acquisition vehicle (courseware): consideration may be cash, common stock, debt or a mix; it may be a one-time lump sum, tied to how well the target performs in future (an earn-out) or paid over an extended period. Factors in choosing the acquisition vehicle or post-closing organisation: cost and formality of the organisation, ease of transferring ownership, continuous existence, management control, convenience of obtaining financial support, ease of assimilation, distribution of earnings, scope of individual responsibility and taxation. The corporate structure is the vehicle most often used because it offers limited liability, continuity of ownership, flexible financing and transaction flexibility (for example a tax-free deal); an ESOP structure can be an easy way to sell a small privately held business to employees with tax benefits.

Post-closing organisation (courseware): the post-closing organisation can be the same as the acquisition vehicle or different, such as a divisional or holding company structure. The acquirer picks a structure that makes integration easier, reduces risk from known and unknown liabilities of the target, minimises taxes, passes through losses to shelter owners taxes, keeps the target independent for the duration of an earn-out, preserves unique target characteristics or keeps the tax-free status. A corporate or divisional structure gives the greatest control and immediate integration. Joint ventures and partnerships spread decision-making and slow action. Where the target has large liabilities, an earn-out is needed, the target is a foreign corporation or the acquirer is a financial investor, a holding company can isolate obligations in the subsidiary so that the parent is not put into bankruptcy. A partnership or LLP structure passes operating losses, tax credits and loss carry-forwards to the owners but raises the possibility of double taxation.

Cash payment (courseware): cash suits a target with a large borrowing capacity, a high credit rating or cheap shares, and an acquirer that wants to keep control or avoid dilution. A high-rated acquirer with cheap borrowing is likely to finance cash by borrowing. Highly leveraged acquirers offer less cash, and are more likely to offer a mix of cash and stock. Cash also avoids diluting the voting control of the acquirer shareholders. Acquirers with large cash holdings are more inclined to make cash offers, according to the courseware.

Stock payment (courseware): stock suits an acquirer that believes the target is overvalued, has limited borrowing capacity or surplus cash, or expects integration to need a long time during which cash is needed for investment. Acquirers whose actual leverage is higher than desired use stock. Stock also makes sense when the target value is hard to determine (intangibles, new products, research spending) because the seller shares the future upside and downside; the seller may not insist on an overpriced bid. The seller bears the risk that the acquirer shares are overvalued, and sellers may demand stock so that they can postpone tax. Debt is less appealing to sellers because the acquirer may default and the market for the securities of unlisted firms is illiquid. Acquirers with more affordable debt may borrow to pay cash and may bid higher.

Mix of cash and stock, and convertibles (courseware): giving target shareholders a choice among payments motivates more to take part in a tender offer; some prefer cash to pay tax on the sale, others prefer stock. A mixed offer with an option for each holder makes the total cash required unpredictable, which can be solved by a proration clause in the agreement or tender offer: if more holders elect cash than the agreed cash pool, each electing holder receives a proportionate part in cash. A shared overvaluation (acquirer stock price above intrinsic value) may be reduced after merger as the combined firm lower leverage cuts the cost of capital. Convertible securities help when both sides lack information: they give the target holders a floor value (the debt value at maturity plus accrued interest) and a share in future upside through conversion, while the acquirer does not dilute ownership at once; bondholders convert only if the stock price rises above the conversion price, otherwise the instrument remains debt.

Tax and accounting considerations (courseware): accounting concerns affect reported earnings of the combined firm and tax considerations decide whether a transaction is taxable to the target shareholders; the core economics of the deal should drive the decision, with tax benefits only reinforcing it. Buyers care about the tax basis of acquired assets and about avoiding hidden target tax liabilities; sellers care about postponing tax. A transaction is taxable to the target shareholders if the majority of consideration is cash, debt or something other than equity: a cash purchase of assets, a cash purchase of shares, and a statutory cash merger or consolidation are examples. In a direct statutory merger, assets and liabilities pass to the surviving company; a triangular merger puts the target into a subsidiary of the acquirer, shielding the acquirer from the target liabilities (forward triangular: target merges into the subsidiary; reverse triangular: subsidiary merges into the target).

Step-up, double taxation and tax-free deals (courseware): in a taxable purchase of assets the tax basis of the acquired assets is stepped up to fair market value (the purchase price less assumed liabilities), which gives extra depreciation and lower tax in later years; the seller recognises a gain on assets (fair market value less net book value). Double taxation can arise if the target pays tax on gains and its shareholders are then taxed again when the proceeds are distributed or the firm is liquidated. In a taxable purchase of target stock, the transaction is between the acquirer and the target shareholders, so there is no tax at the company level and no step-up unless an election is made. A transaction where the target shareholders receive mainly acquirer stock is generally tax-free to them at the time (gain is deferred); any non-equity consideration (boot) is taxed as regular income. To be tax-free, the courseware (United States rules) requires continuity of ownership (a significant portion of consideration in acquirer stock), continuity of business enterprise, and a legitimate business purpose, and the deal must not be part of a wider scheme resembling a tax-free reorganisation. Net operating losses may be carried forward and used by an acquirer, subject to limits.

Tax reliefs in amalgamation in India (courseware, principles only): where an amalgamation meets the statutory conditions (a scheme within the Income-tax Act definition and an amalgamated company that is an Indian company), the transfer of assets by the amalgamating company is not treated as a transfer for capital gains, the shareholders exchanging shares for shares of the amalgamated company are exempt from capital gains on the exchange, and the cost of the new shares is related to the cost of the old. Carry forward and set-off of the accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation of the amalgamating company is available only to specified types of undertaking and only if conditions on continuing the business and the use of assets are met; if they are not, the benefit is withdrawn. The courseware notes that MAT credit available to the amalgamating company has no express provision for carry forward in the amalgamated company. Domestic tax issues arise over cash or securities paid to shareholders and part payment to shareholders of a demerged company; cross-border issues arise because countries can both tax the same income, so the availability of double taxation avoidance agreements (DTAAs) matters, though these can be changed. The conditions, section numbers and percentages are not taught.

Financial reporting of business combinations (courseware): the acquisition method is applied to each business combination: identify the acquirer, determine the acquisition date, recognise and measure the identifiable assets acquired, the liabilities assumed and any non-controlling interest in the acquiree, and recognise and measure goodwill or a gain from a bargain purchase. Under Ind AS the acquired assets, liabilities and contingent liabilities are recorded at fair value at the acquisition date and the excess is goodwill; goodwill represents expected future economic gains from assets not individually identified. In consolidated statements 100 per cent of the target assets and liabilities is recorded even if the acquirer buys less (for example 50.1 per cent), and the non-controlling interest (the part not bought) is shown separately in equity; the income statement includes 100 per cent of the target revenues and expenses, with the share of net income attributable to non-controlling holders shown separately. In a share acquisition no intangible assets are recognised in the standalone books of the target; they are recognised in the consolidated statements at acquisition-date fair value.

Deal financing (courseware): deals are financed by cash, stock, debt or a combination. The choice depends on the state of the capital markets, the liquidity and creditworthiness of both firms, the combined borrowing capacity, the size of the deal and the target shareholders preference for cash or shares. An acquirer can decouple financing from the bid by issuing shares in advance to investors who are told that proceeds finance acquisitions; timing share issues when the stock is richly valued raises the value of the deal to the acquirer in the short run. Options: issue of equity or preference shares; internal accruals; long-term loans from banks or lenders; issue of convertible or non-convertible debentures or other domestic or foreign debt. Debt gives the benefit of the interest tax shield and often higher earnings per share and return on equity, but excessive debt raises the risk of financial distress and limits investment flexibility. Merging companies whose cash flows are uncorrelated tend to increase leverage after the merger because the combined cash flow is steadier. Senior debt has priority over junior (subordinated) debt, which ranks lower and is unsecured; convertible bonds can be converted into shares at a predefined ratio, usually at a coupon below the straight-debt rate; conversion dilutes current holders. An indenture is the contract that sets out how the principal will be repaid and the affirmative and negative covenants; credit rating agencies rate debt according to the consistency of earnings, interest coverage, debt to total capital, subordination and the history of debt service.

Cross-border acquisition finance in India (courseware, structure only): inbound acquisitions (a foreign acquirer buys shares of an Indian target) and outbound acquisitions (an Indian acquirer buys a foreign target, directly or through an offshore special purpose vehicle). For an inbound deal the loan market is mostly overseas: the acquirer commonly sets up an offshore SPV that borrows against its own assets and shareholdings and invests in the Indian target through foreign direct investment; a foreign owned and controlled company (FOCC) in India is not permitted to leverage in the Indian market to buy shares, so it issues non-convertible debentures (NCDs) subscribed by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). For an outbound deal the Indian acquirer may raise domestic funds subject to central bank rules, borrow abroad (external commercial borrowing), or use an offshore SPV that borrows from offshore lenders. Domestic acquisitions are usually financed by NCDs or loans from non-banking financial companies and funds. Loan agreements for cross-border financing are commonly based on market standard forms (the Asia Pacific Loan Market Association or the Loan Market Association). Specific restrictions and eligibility are not taught.

payload.title: Deal structure and the negotiation
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **deal structure** is the **agreement between acquirer and target** on their **rights and obligations**, reached by **negotiation** after the strategy, target choice and financial analysis are done.

Structuring decides **how risk is shared** and how many of each party goals are met, including **how much of the target liabilities the acquirer takes on**. **Risk moved out of one place tends to reappear in another** (the courseware image is **squeezing a water balloon**).

**Main aspects:** the **acquisition vehicle and post-closing organisation**, the **form of acquisition**, the **form of payment** and the **legal form of the seller**. **Financing, tax and structure are interwoven**, and **private equity and hedge funds** often help finance leveraged deals. The aim is a **mutually beneficial (win-win)** outcome.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A deal that looks cheap but leaves all risk with one side is unlikely to close.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a deal structure specify?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The rights and obligations of the acquirer and the target, including how risk is shared.

payload.title: Choosing the acquisition vehicle and post-closing organisation
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Consideration** can be **cash, stock, debt or a mix**, as a **lump sum**, tied to future performance (**earn-out**) or **paid over time**.

**Factors in the choice of vehicle:** **cost and formality**, **ease of transferring ownership**, **continuity**, **management control**, **ease of raising finance**, **ease of assimilation**, **distribution of earnings**, **personal liability** and **tax**.

**Corporate structure** is the most used: **limited liability**, **continuity**, **flexible financing**. An **ESOP** can sell a small private business to **employees** with tax benefits.

**Post-closing options:** a **corporate or divisional** structure gives the **most control and quick integration**; **joint ventures and partnerships** **slow decisions**. A **holding company** isolates **target liabilities**, suits **earn-outs**, **foreign targets** and **financial investors**. A **partnership or LLP** passes **losses and credits** to owners but may bring **double taxation**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The best vehicle depends on which risk and tax attributes the buyer most wants to keep.

self_check.prompt_text: Why might an acquirer use a holding company for a target with large liabilities?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It can isolate the obligations in the subsidiary so that the parent is protected from the target bankruptcy.

payload.title: Paying in cash or in stock
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Cash is favoured when | Stock is favoured when |
| --- | --- |
| The **acquirer wants control** and no **dilution** | The acquirer thinks the **target is overvalued** |
| The acquirer has **high credit rating and cheap borrowing** or **large cash** | The acquirer has **limited borrowing capacity** or its **leverage is already high** |
| The target has **large borrowing capacity** or **cheap shares** | The acquirer needs **cash for integration** spending |
|  | The **target value is hard to judge** (intangibles, new products): the **seller shares upside and downside** |

**Sellers** may prefer stock to **postpone tax**, but bear the risk that the **acquirer stock is overvalued**. **Debt** is less appealing to sellers because of **default risk** and **illiquid** securities.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Stock transfers some valuation risk from the buyer to the seller.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does paying in stock suit a target whose value is hard to determine?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The sellers share in the later gains or losses, which narrows disagreement about value.

payload.title: Mixed offers, proration and convertibles
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Mixed offers** attract more target holders because some prefer **cash** (to pay tax) and others **stock**. A **choice** makes the **total cash needed unpredictable**.

**Proration clause:** if elections for cash exceed the **cash pool**, each electing holder receives **cash pool / cash elected** as a fraction of the cash requested, the rest in stock.

**Convertibles** help when **both sides lack information**: they give the target holders a **floor value** (**debt value at maturity plus accrued interest**) and a **share of future upside** if the price rises above the **conversion price**; otherwise they stay **debt**.

**Conversion ratio = face value / conversion price**; **conversion value = ratio x current share price**.

assumptions: Each electing holder is treated alike
common_errors: Dividing by the pool instead of the elections
Forgetting the balance is paid in stock

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Without proration the acquirer could face an unlimited cash demand.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a proration clause give the acquirer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A cap on total cash paid, because over-subscribed cash elections are scaled back.

payload.title: Tax considerations and the shape of the deal
payload.core_explanation_md:
**The core economics decide the deal; tax benefits only reinforce it.** The **buyer** cares about the **tax basis of acquired assets** and **hidden tax liabilities**; the **seller** about **postponing tax**.

**Taxable to target holders:** most of the consideration is **cash, debt or other non-equity**: **cash purchase of assets or shares**, **cash statutory merger**.

**Triangular merger:** the target is combined with an **acquirer subsidiary**, shielding the **acquirer from the target liabilities**: **forward** (target merges into the subsidiary) or **reverse** (subsidiary merges into the target).

**Asset purchase:** **step-up** of asset basis to **fair market value** gives **extra depreciation and lower later tax**, but the seller may face **double taxation** (company tax, then tax on distributing the proceeds).

**Stock purchase:** **no company-level tax** and **no step-up** unless elected.

**Tax-free (courseware, United States rules):** **mainly acquirer stock**, **continuity of ownership**, **continuity of business**, a **legitimate business purpose**. Non-equity consideration (**boot**) is taxed. **Tax losses** may be used by the acquirer subject to limits.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A tax saving that is the only reason for a deal can make the deal fail the tests for tax-free treatment.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the main benefit to the buyer of a taxable asset purchase?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The assets are stepped up to fair value, giving more depreciation and lower tax later.

payload.title: Value of the tax step-up
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Step-up** = **fair market value paid for the asset - tax basis before**.

**Annual tax saving from extra depreciation = step-up / depreciable life x tax rate.**

The **present value** of these savings is a **benefit of an asset deal** that the buyer may share with the seller through a **higher price**; it is offset by the **seller extra tax** on the gain.

variables.name: Increase in the tax basis of the asset

assumptions: Taxable profits are large enough to use the deduction
common_errors: Using the whole asset value instead of the step-up

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A longer life spreads the same total saving over more years.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the annual tax saving from a step-up?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Step-up divided by the life, multiplied by the tax rate.

payload.title: Tax reliefs for amalgamations in India (principles)
payload.core_explanation_md:
For an amalgamation that meets the **statutory conditions**:

- **No capital gains** arise on **transfer of assets** to the **Indian amalgamated company**.
- **Shareholders** swapping shares for shares of the Indian amalgamated company are **exempt from capital gains** on the exchange.
- **Accumulated losses and unabsorbed depreciation** carry forward **only for specified undertakings** and **only if conditions** on **continuing the business** and **use of assets** are met; otherwise the benefit is **withdrawn**.
- The courseware notes **no express provision** to carry forward **MAT credit** to the amalgamated company.

**Issues:** **cash or securities** paid to holders and **part payment to demerged company holders**. **Cross-border:** **double taxation** arises when two countries tax the same income; **DTAAs** reduce it but can be **amended**.

**Sections, percentages and periods are not taught.**
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The reliefs exist to stop a genuine reorganisation from being taxed as a sale.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do double taxation avoidance agreements matter in cross-border deals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They limit the overlapping claims of two countries to tax the same income.

payload.title: Acquisition method: goodwill and non-controlling interest
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Steps:** identify the **acquirer**; fix the **acquisition date**; recognise and measure **identifiable assets, liabilities and any non-controlling interest (NCI)**; recognise **goodwill or a bargain purchase gain**.

**Goodwill = consideration transferred + NCI - fair value of identifiable net assets** (if positive). If **negative**, it is a **gain from a bargain purchase**.

**Consolidation shows 100 per cent** of the target **assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses**, even when the acquirer buys **50.1 per cent**. The **part not owned** appears as **NCI in equity**, and **profit attributable to NCI** is shown separately.

In a **share acquisition** the target standalone books do not record intangibles; the **consolidated statements** record them at **acquisition-date fair value**.

variables.name: Fair value of identifiable net assets

assumptions: Fair values are measured at the acquisition date
NCI is measured at the chosen basis
common_errors: Using book values of the target assets
Leaving NCI out of the calculation

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Goodwill is the premium paid for gains that are not tied to any single identified asset.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the income of a 60 per cent owned subsidiary shown in consolidated accounts?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In full, with the share belonging to the other 40 per cent shown as attributable to NCI.

payload.title: Financing a deal: sources and debt features
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Choice of finance** depends on **capital market state**, **liquidity and credit standing** of both firms, **combined borrowing capacity**, **deal size** and **target holders preference**.

**Sources:** **equity or preference shares**, **internal accruals**, **long-term bank loans**, **convertible or non-convertible debentures** and other **domestic or foreign debt**.

**Decoupling:** an acquirer can **raise equity beforehand** from investors told that the proceeds will finance acquisitions; issuing when **shares are richly valued** helps.

**Debt:** gives an **interest tax shield** and **often higher EPS and ROE**, but **too much** raises **distress risk** and **limits flexibility**. **Merging firms with uncorrelated cash flows** can carry **more debt** afterwards.

**Senior debt** ranks ahead of **subordinated (junior)** debt, which is **unsecured**. **Convertible** bonds convert at a **set ratio**, usually carry a **lower coupon** and **dilute** owners on conversion. The **indenture** sets out **repayment, affirmative and negative covenants**. **Rating** depends on **earnings consistency, interest cover, debt to total capital, subordination and repayment history**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Seniority matters because it decides who is paid first if the combined firm fails.

self_check.prompt_text: What is an indenture?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The contract setting out how the debt will be repaid and the covenants the borrower must observe.

payload.title: Comparing financing by equity and by debt
payload.core_explanation_md:
**After-tax cost of debt = interest rate x (1 - tax rate).**

**EPS with equity financing** = **(earnings) / (existing shares + new shares)**, where **new shares = amount raised / issue price**.

**EPS with debt financing** = **(earnings - interest x (1 - tax rate)) / existing shares**.

**Interest cover = EBIT / interest.**

Debt often gives the **higher EPS**, but **cover falls** and **risk rises**. EPS alone is not a test of value.

assumptions: The firm has enough profit to use the deduction
common_errors: Using the pre-tax rate in the comparison

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The tax shield lowers the effective cost of debt below the interest rate.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the after-tax cost of debt below its interest rate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest is tax deductible, so the government bears part of the cost.

payload.title: Financing cross-border and domestic acquisitions in India
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Inbound** (foreign acquirer, Indian target): the loan market is **mostly overseas**. A common route is an **offshore SPV** that **borrows abroad** and **invests via foreign direct investment**. A **foreign owned and controlled company (FOCC)** in India **cannot leverage domestically** to buy shares, so it issues **non-convertible debentures (NCDs)** to **foreign portfolio investors**.

**Outbound** (Indian acquirer, foreign target): **domestic funds** (subject to central bank rules), **external commercial borrowing**, or an **offshore SPV** borrowing from offshore lenders.

**Domestic:** mainly **NCDs** and **loans from non-banking finance companies and funds**.

Cross-border loan agreements often follow **market standard forms** (the **LMA** or **APLMA**). **Specific limits, eligibility and rules are not taught**; they change and must be checked at the time.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The same acquisition can be financed through several different routes, each with its own rules.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does an inbound acquirer often use an offshore special purpose vehicle?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To raise finance in overseas markets against its own assets and then invest in the Indian target.

items.title: Deal structure and the negotiation
items.core_explanation_md:
A **deal structure** is the **agreement between acquirer and target** on their **rights and obligations**, reached by **negotiation** after the strategy, target choice and financial analysis are done.

Structuring decides **how risk is shared** and how many of each party goals are met, including **how much of the target liabilities the acquirer takes on**. **Risk moved out of one place tends to reappear in another** (the courseware image is **squeezing a water balloon**).

**Main aspects:** the **acquisition vehicle and post-closing organisation**, the **form of acquisition**, the **form of payment** and the **legal form of the seller**. **Financing, tax and structure are interwoven**, and **private equity and hedge funds** often help finance leveraged deals. The aim is a **mutually beneficial (win-win)** outcome.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A deal that looks cheap but leaves all risk with one side is unlikely to close.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a deal structure specify?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The rights and obligations of the acquirer and the target, including how risk is shared.

items.title: Choosing the acquisition vehicle and post-closing organisation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Consideration** can be **cash, stock, debt or a mix**, as a **lump sum**, tied to future performance (**earn-out**) or **paid over time**.

**Factors in the choice of vehicle:** **cost and formality**, **ease of transferring ownership**, **continuity**, **management control**, **ease of raising finance**, **ease of assimilation**, **distribution of earnings**, **personal liability** and **tax**.

**Corporate structure** is the most used: **limited liability**, **continuity**, **flexible financing**. An **ESOP** can sell a small private business to **employees** with tax benefits.

**Post-closing options:** a **corporate or divisional** structure gives the **most control and quick integration**; **joint ventures and partnerships** **slow decisions**. A **holding company** isolates **target liabilities**, suits **earn-outs**, **foreign targets** and **financial investors**. A **partnership or LLP** passes **losses and credits** to owners but may bring **double taxation**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The best vehicle depends on which risk and tax attributes the buyer most wants to keep.

self_check.expected_takeaway: It can isolate the obligations in the subsidiary so that the parent is protected from the target bankruptcy.

items.title: Paying in cash or in stock
items.core_explanation_md:
| Cash is favoured when | Stock is favoured when |
| --- | --- |
| The **acquirer wants control** and no **dilution** | The acquirer thinks the **target is overvalued** |
| The acquirer has **high credit rating and cheap borrowing** or **large cash** | The acquirer has **limited borrowing capacity** or its **leverage is already high** |
| The target has **large borrowing capacity** or **cheap shares** | The acquirer needs **cash for integration** spending |
|  | The **target value is hard to judge** (intangibles, new products): the **seller shares upside and downside** |

**Sellers** may prefer stock to **postpone tax**, but bear the risk that the **acquirer stock is overvalued**. **Debt** is less appealing to sellers because of **default risk** and **illiquid** securities.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Stock transfers some valuation risk from the buyer to the seller.

items.title: Mixed offers, proration and convertibles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Mixed offers** attract more target holders because some prefer **cash** (to pay tax) and others **stock**. A **choice** makes the **total cash needed unpredictable**.

**Proration clause:** if elections for cash exceed the **cash pool**, each electing holder receives **cash pool / cash elected** as a fraction of the cash requested, the rest in stock.

**Convertibles** help when **both sides lack information**: they give the target holders a **floor value** (**debt value at maturity plus accrued interest**) and a **share of future upside** if the price rises above the **conversion price**; otherwise they stay **debt**.

**Conversion ratio = face value / conversion price**; **conversion value = ratio x current share price**.

items.title: Tax considerations and the shape of the deal
items.core_explanation_md:
**The core economics decide the deal; tax benefits only reinforce it.** The **buyer** cares about the **tax basis of acquired assets** and **hidden tax liabilities**; the **seller** about **postponing tax**.

**Taxable to target holders:** most of the consideration is **cash, debt or other non-equity**: **cash purchase of assets or shares**, **cash statutory merger**.

**Triangular merger:** the target is combined with an **acquirer subsidiary**, shielding the **acquirer from the target liabilities**: **forward** (target merges into the subsidiary) or **reverse** (subsidiary merges into the target).

**Asset purchase:** **step-up** of asset basis to **fair market value** gives **extra depreciation and lower later tax**, but the seller may face **double taxation** (company tax, then tax on distributing the proceeds).

**Stock purchase:** **no company-level tax** and **no step-up** unless elected.

**Tax-free (courseware, United States rules):** **mainly acquirer stock**, **continuity of ownership**, **continuity of business**, a **legitimate business purpose**. Non-equity consideration (**boot**) is taxed. **Tax losses** may be used by the acquirer subject to limits.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A tax saving that is the only reason for a deal can make the deal fail the tests for tax-free treatment.

items.title: Value of the tax step-up
items.core_explanation_md:
**Step-up** = **fair market value paid for the asset - tax basis before**.

**Annual tax saving from extra depreciation = step-up / depreciable life x tax rate.**

The **present value** of these savings is a **benefit of an asset deal** that the buyer may share with the seller through a **higher price**; it is offset by the **seller extra tax** on the gain.

items.core_explanation_md:
For an amalgamation that meets the **statutory conditions**:

- **No capital gains** arise on **transfer of assets** to the **Indian amalgamated company**.
- **Shareholders** swapping shares for shares of the Indian amalgamated company are **exempt from capital gains** on the exchange.
- **Accumulated losses and unabsorbed depreciation** carry forward **only for specified undertakings** and **only if conditions** on **continuing the business** and **use of assets** are met; otherwise the benefit is **withdrawn**.
- The courseware notes **no express provision** to carry forward **MAT credit** to the amalgamated company.

**Issues:** **cash or securities** paid to holders and **part payment to demerged company holders**. **Cross-border:** **double taxation** arises when two countries tax the same income; **DTAAs** reduce it but can be **amended**.

**Sections, percentages and periods are not taught.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: The reliefs exist to stop a genuine reorganisation from being taxed as a sale.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do double taxation avoidance agreements matter in cross-border deals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They limit the overlapping claims of two countries to tax the same income.

items.title: Acquisition method: goodwill and non-controlling interest
items.core_explanation_md:
**Steps:** identify the **acquirer**; fix the **acquisition date**; recognise and measure **identifiable assets, liabilities and any non-controlling interest (NCI)**; recognise **goodwill or a bargain purchase gain**.

**Goodwill = consideration transferred + NCI - fair value of identifiable net assets** (if positive). If **negative**, it is a **gain from a bargain purchase**.

**Consolidation shows 100 per cent** of the target **assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses**, even when the acquirer buys **50.1 per cent**. The **part not owned** appears as **NCI in equity**, and **profit attributable to NCI** is shown separately.

In a **share acquisition** the target standalone books do not record intangibles; the **consolidated statements** record them at **acquisition-date fair value**.

items.title: Financing a deal: sources and debt features
items.core_explanation_md:
**Choice of finance** depends on **capital market state**, **liquidity and credit standing** of both firms, **combined borrowing capacity**, **deal size** and **target holders preference**.

**Sources:** **equity or preference shares**, **internal accruals**, **long-term bank loans**, **convertible or non-convertible debentures** and other **domestic or foreign debt**.

**Decoupling:** an acquirer can **raise equity beforehand** from investors told that the proceeds will finance acquisitions; issuing when **shares are richly valued** helps.

**Debt:** gives an **interest tax shield** and **often higher EPS and ROE**, but **too much** raises **distress risk** and **limits flexibility**. **Merging firms with uncorrelated cash flows** can carry **more debt** afterwards.

**Senior debt** ranks ahead of **subordinated (junior)** debt, which is **unsecured**. **Convertible** bonds convert at a **set ratio**, usually carry a **lower coupon** and **dilute** owners on conversion. The **indenture** sets out **repayment, affirmative and negative covenants**. **Rating** depends on **earnings consistency, interest cover, debt to total capital, subordination and repayment history**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Seniority matters because it decides who is paid first if the combined firm fails.

self_check.prompt_text: What is an indenture?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The contract setting out how the debt will be repaid and the covenants the borrower must observe.

items.title: Comparing financing by equity and by debt
items.core_explanation_md:
**After-tax cost of debt = interest rate x (1 - tax rate).**

**EPS with equity financing** = **(earnings) / (existing shares + new shares)**, where **new shares = amount raised / issue price**.

**EPS with debt financing** = **(earnings - interest x (1 - tax rate)) / existing shares**.

**Interest cover = EBIT / interest.**

Debt often gives the **higher EPS**, but **cover falls** and **risk rises**. EPS alone is not a test of value.

items.title: Financing cross-border and domestic acquisitions in India
items.core_explanation_md:
**Inbound** (foreign acquirer, Indian target): the loan market is **mostly overseas**. A common route is an **offshore SPV** that **borrows abroad** and **invests via foreign direct investment**. A **foreign owned and controlled company (FOCC)** in India **cannot leverage domestically** to buy shares, so it issues **non-convertible debentures (NCDs)** to **foreign portfolio investors**.

**Outbound** (Indian acquirer, foreign target): **domestic funds** (subject to central bank rules), **external commercial borrowing**, or an **offshore SPV** borrowing from offshore lenders.

**Domestic:** mainly **NCDs** and **loans from non-banking finance companies and funds**.

Cross-border loan agreements often follow **market standard forms** (the **LMA** or **APLMA**). **Specific limits, eligibility and rules are not taught**; they change and must be checked at the time.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The same acquisition can be financed through several different routes, each with its own rules.

self_check.expected_takeaway: To raise finance in overseas markets against its own assets and then invest in the Indian target.
